articles.title_orig: Binance Hack Sends Crypto Stocks Tumbling
articles.title_zh: Binance Hack Sends Crypto Stocks Tumbling
articles.content_orig:
Binance said Friday that a security incident impacted about $6.3 billion in client assets, with around $3 billion frozen on-chain, marking the largest crypto hack on record.
The company later added it began recovering assets impacted by the breach after pledging to cover losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users, which the company created in 2018 as a protection for clients in the event of a hack.
It wasn't clear how the attack took place. The world's largest crypto exchange initially said the hack may involve "a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions." However, Co-CEO Richard Teng later said the attack involved a more complex process rather than the misuse of a single engineer's permissions.
The FBI said Friday it was aware of the incident and was in touch with "relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate ​potential impacts, ​and ⁠coordinate appropriate investigative steps."
It wasn't clear either who was responsible for the breach. But TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence and AI investigations company, pointed to North Korean hackers as the potential culprits . "Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack and the KelpDAO hack in April 2026: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet, staging that began well before the theft, and signatures obtained in advance then executed in one burst," the company said in a post.
Blockchain data platform Chainalysis also said this appears "be the work of North Korean cybercrime group TraderTraitor . This group has repeatedly targeted the cryptocurrency industry, exchanges, DeFi protocols, and investors, to raise funds for the regime. We base our intelligence assessment on on-chain activity observed in the hours following the hack."
Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals while it overhauls its withdrawal security systems and has revoked the affected address authorizations, Teng said. The exchange is also working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms to trace and recover the stolen funds, while deposits remain unaffected.
Binance co-founder Yi He said deposits remained unaffected and continued to operate normally, while the exchange was working on enhancements to its withdrawal service and related address controls. It expects to begin resuming withdrawal services within the next 48 hours.
"We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak. We will share a detailed technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete and the facts are fully verified," Binance said.
The announcement followed moves by several crypto firms, including Circle Internet Group , Tether and Ripple, to freeze funds tied to the hack.
Exploits are not uncommon in the crypto space. In 2025, Bybit suffered roughly $1.5 billion in losses due to a hack. More recently, Bitget lost more than $350 million worth of digital assets in a cyber theft incident. Over the past several years, bad actors have also drained billions of dollars in crypto from decentralized exchanges.
This week's breach "proves our exact point in proposing regulations for crypto markets earlier this month," Michael Selig, chairman of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, said Friday in a CNBC "Squawk on the Street" interview. The U.S. derivatives regulator on Oct. 5 proposed a framework that would effectively put crypto exchanges under federal government oversight — after Congress failed to approve legislation to regulate the asset.
"The real issue here is that these are unregulated offshore exchanges, and they don't have the same sorts of safeguards that we have in our financial markets here in the United States. We want to offer a federal option to these exchanges to come and register with the CFTC, and they would be subject to the same sorts of cyber security safeguards that we have in our markets today," he said.
Bitcoin fell more than 4% to $77,187.60 on Friday as the hack weighed on crypto markets.
Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire said Thursday evening in a social media post that the company had frozen more than 800 million in USD Coin associated with the incident. USDT stablecoin issuer Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino also said in on X that his firm had frozen more than 1.5 billion of its stablecoin that may have been related to a potential breach.
Jack McDonald, Ripple's senior vice president of stablecoins, said it was actively freezing affected funds held in RLUSD, its U.S. dollar-backed stablecoin.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Pakistan military 'cautiously optimistic' on Iran-US mediation
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Pakistan military 'cautiously optimistic' on Iran-US mediation
articles.content_orig:
Pakistan’s army is “cautiously optimistic” ⁠about mediation efforts between Iran and the United States as regional countries seek to revive a ceasefire in the eight-month-old war.
Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, spokesman for Pakistan’s military, suggested on Friday that there were positive signs in attempts to de-escalate the conflict. His comments to the Reuters news agency were the first since a high-level delegation visited Tehran this week.
Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, Pakistan’s chief mediator, has been to Tehran twice this month, most recently on Monday, alongside Saudi and Turkish officials.
“Why would the Field Marshal be going twice if it is not for some positivity? So yes, of course,” Chaudhry said when asked whether the trips were a positive ⁠sign.
“The word that we would use is always cautiously optimistic,” added Chaudhry, director general of Inter-Services Public Relations.
He also warned that there are parties seeking to obstruct mediation between the US and Iran.
There are still “powerful spoilers and detractors” who believe conflict serves them, he added without naming them.
Speaking in the garrison city of Rawalpindi, where Pakistan’s armed forces are headquartered, Chaudhry declined to say what was discussed in Tehran or whether the US had backed the trip.
His comments on Friday came as Qatari mediators arrived in Tehran in another apparent bid to negotiate a revival of the June ceasefire that collapsed months later.
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin joined Pakistan’s Munir in ‌Tehran on Monday.
Their two countries signed a joint defence pact with Pakistan on August 7, saying an attack on any signatory will be treated as an attack on all.
The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement has taken on added significance as the Iran war has redrawn regional alliances and raised fears of a broader Middle East conflict.
While the three signatories say the agreement is aimed at collective deterrence and regional security, analysts see its evolution as closely tied to efforts by regional powers to manage the fallout from the Iran-US confrontation.
After Monday’s talks, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said regional security should be ensured by regional countries without foreign intervention.
The wording of the pact does not bar new ⁠members, Chaudhry said on Friday when asked whether Iran could join.
“Anyone who has a shared vision of collective deterrence ⁠and regional peace, why not? Everyone is most welcome,” he said, adding that it was for the political leadership of the three principal parties to decide.
Asked whether more Pakistani troops were being sent to Saudi Arabia under the agreement, Chaudhry said that would depend on the situation and the decision of both countries’ political leadership.
He said Pakistan was committed to defending Saudi ⁠Arabia and the holy sites of Mecca and Medina. “We are not part of the Yemeni conflict, which is an intra-Yemen conflict,” he added.
Fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi group has been reignited by the Iran ⁠conflict, stoking fears of a wider war.

articles.title_orig: Meta Settles Social Media Addiction Case, Avoiding Trial
articles.title_zh: Meta Settles Social Media Addiction Case, Avoiding Trial
articles.content_orig:
Meta has settled a social media addiction lawsuit , resolving claims against the technology giant before the case was set to go to trial next month, according to a lawyer for one of the plaintiffs.
The suit was brought by an 18-year-old woman identified in court documents as K.D.B. who alleged that Meta and Snapchat parent company Snap, which remains a defendant in the case, designed their social media platforms to foster addictive behavior. Another plaintiff in the lawsuit, dubbed S.J., settled with Meta last week.
Terms of Meta's settlement were not disclosed.
S.J. and K.D.B. also originally sued TikTok and Alphabet's YouTube platform, which each separately settled before trial.
The plaintiffs claim that the social media platforms contributed to their mental health struggles.
A spokesperson for the Lanier Law Firm, which is representing the plaintiffs, said they will proceed with their complaint against Snap.
"Each plaintiff alleges that Snap designed Snapchat to maximize the time young users spend on the app, using features such as Snapstreaks, Snapscores, push notifications, and filters, and that their compulsive use of Snapchat caused and contributed to severe mental and physical health injuries, including depression, anxiety, an eating disorder, and self-harm," the spokesperson said.
Snap disputes the allegations and has defended the company's practices.
Jury selection began this week in Los Angeles, with opening statements expected to begin in early November. Lawyers for the plaintiffs have said they expect the trial to last into mid-December.
"We remain committed to improving safety for kids on social media apps and holding tech companies accountable, and we are pleased to have brought this matter to a just resolution on behalf of our client," Emily Jeffcott, the trial counsel for K.D.B., said in a statement.
A spokesperson for Meta, which still faces similar litigation alleging that its social platforms harm users' mental health, said the company will continue to defend itself in court.
"Trials, dismissals and settlements are all common in the bellwether process, and this litigation is no exception," she said in a statement. "We will continue to defend ourselves in court, and we stand by our record. We've spent more than a decade building protections for teens, and our agreement with 52 bipartisan attorneys general goes even further with strict time limits, no access at night, and no notifications during school hours."
In August, Meta agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion to dozens of states that alleged the company used its social platforms, including Facebook and Instagram, to hook young internet users while concealing the risks.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Deepening Tech Selloff Pushes Nasdaq Toward Its Worst Month in Over a Year
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Deepening Tech Selloff Pushes Nasdaq Toward Its Worst Month in Over a Year
articles.content_orig:
By HUGO DUNCAN, BUSINESS EDITOR
Updated: 14:42 EDT, 30 October 2026
A Halloween slump in technology stocks has fuelled fears of a market crash that would hammer the savings and pensions of millions of British families.
On a brutal session in trading rooms in New York, the tech-heavy Nasdaq index followed up Thursday’s 1.4 per cent slide with a drop of more than 3 per cent on Friday.
Analysts warned of ‘tech carnage’ with shares in US giants Amazon and Intel among the biggest losers following bleak results on Thursday night.
Intel shares tumbled nearly 30 per cent – wiping around £90billion off its value – while Amazon fell more than 3 per cent.
The latest sell-off came after Google owner Alphabet tumbled more than 12 per cent on Thursday night – wiping close to £400billion off its value.
The tech titan, one of the so-called Magnificent Seven, is now down 30 per cent since its peak in May while the Nasdaq is off 7.5 per cent - wiping £2.5trillion off its value.
Traders are braced for turmoil on dealing floors around the world
A host of US tech stocks, driven to record highs this year on a wave of AI mania, are now in so-called ‘bear market’ territory – meaning they are down more than 20 per cent from their peak. Some have halved in value.
The FTSE 100 index has held up in the face of the sell-off – at least for now – as it benefits from a lack of exposure to tech and AI.
London’s blue-chip index closed up 7.71 points to 10,729.78 on Friday despite the ructions on Wall Street.
But the tech slump is proving painful for millions of British investors who are exposed to the US stock market through their pensions and Isas.
A host of Britain’s most popular investments, from technology funds and trusts and those that track major global indices, are packed full of US stocks now in reverse.
Neil Wilson, investor strategist at Saxo, warned of ‘tech carnage as October wraps up’ as investors fret over whether huge spending on AI infrastructure such as data centres will pay off.
He said: ‘This is starting to look quite ugly. The selloff looks a bit indiscriminate and shows that investors don't just want capex, they want to see the returns already.’
The AI trade has run into turbulence recently as investors grew uneasy about the billions Big Tech has poured into scaling up AI infrastructure while awaiting evidence of stronger returns.
Several companies have tapped the bond market to finance those investments, amplifying concerns that debt-funded spending will become harder to justify as borrowing costs rise.
Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion, said the slump in share prices in recent days ‘is a good example of how the AI trade has changed’.
He added: ‘At this point, the market isn't just asking how fast you can grow. It's asking what you have to spend to get there.’
The AI trade got a brief respite earlier this week when AI lab Anthropic – which is behind the Claude model – unveiled plans to list on the US stock market with a value of up to £1.5trillion.
Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, said: ‘The FTSE 100’s lack of tech exposure has proved to be a blessing in disguise. The UK index is standing tall amid a global tech sell-off.'
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, described the slump in New York as an 'AI reality check'.
He said: ‘Investors are increasingly unhappy at the huge sums of money being spent on AI infrastructure without a clear roadmap for when, or whether, those investments will deliver a sufficient return. That means investors are questioning if money is being spent wisely.
'Big tech companies are going all-in with their bets that AI will be the biggest thing in decades to transform business and consumer life. If they get that bet wrong, the fallout could be huge.'
He added: 'Tech stocks have gone from being investors’ main feast to stale bread.
'For years, investors have treated tech as the golden ticket to wealth creation, and for a long time they have been richly rewarded. That enthusiasm is now evaporating, and some investors are racing for the exit.
'The gigantic declines we’ve seen this week in shares such as Alphabet and Intel suggest that investor sentiment has been turned on its head. Current price action implies tech investors want to jump off the treadmill rather than slow it down.'
The top ten holdings of the highly popular Vanguard FTSE All World ET highlight how much big US tech shares matter to UK investors
Millions of British savers are exposed to US tech stocks – even if they don’t know it.
Companies such as Nvidia, Alphabet, Apple, Meta, Amazon and Intel are held in countless global funds that form the backbone of pension savings.
When these stocks go south, so can the value of the nest eggs held by workers and pensioners alike.
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said: ‘The tech sell-off matters to investors around the world as the AI theme has weaved its way into countless sectors and geographies.
‘In particular, the US stock market is home to the giant tech names and is a major component of global funds that fill so many people’s investment portfolios.
‘This means that investors might find they have big tech exposure without realising it.’
He points out that 15 years ago, the US represented half of the MSCI World benchmark for the global stock market. It now stands at 73 per cent.
Tech is the dominant sector, making up more than 30 per cent of the index.
‘If tech goes off the boil, global funds might not provide the diversification support some investors expect,’ said Coatsworth.
For those who want to ‘dial down tech exposure’, he suggested switching into a global equity fund that excludes the US.
He pointed investors towards the iShares MSCI World ex-US ETF, which invests in a basket of companies from around the world excluding the US.
Tech stocks only account for 10.9 per cent of the portfolio, with financials the dominant sector at 27.9 per cent and industrials at 17.6 per cent.
‘The main holdings include banks, healthcare companies, oil producers and miners,’ said Coatsworth.
‘That would provide more sector balance and less dependence on tech, but it would mean some of the key names that have led the US market rally in recent years like Nvidia no longer being in the driving seat.’

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq plunges 3%, heads for worst day since June as tech stocks lead sell-off: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq plunges 3%, heads for worst day since June as tech stocks lead sell-off: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
The Nasdaq Composite Index tumbled more than 970 points, or 3.7%, in afternoon trading, while other U.S. financial markets also swooned as investors pulled back amid growing concerns about the health of the critical technology sector.
Intel's stock plunged more than 30%, while shares of Google's parent, Alphabet, continued to wobble after the company's Class A stock slid more than 12% on Thursday, its worst day since the company went public as Google in 2004. The drop erased roughly $500 billion in Alphabet's market value.
Shares of Nvidia, the maker of advanced chips used to power AI models and a bellwether for the sector, also dropped 5%.
"This has been one of the worst tech earnings seasons in memory, with underwhelming results from a slew of very prominent companies," market analyst Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, said in a research note.
"The slump in tech stocks (and the attendant deterioration in tech sentiment) isn't simply a financial phenomenon and could undermine industry fundamentals by making it more difficult for companies to raise incremental debt and equity," he added in a separate report.
The negative sentiment around tech spread to other major stock indices on Friday. The S&P 500 shed 183 points, or 2.4%, while the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average sank 746 points, or 1.4%.
The weaker-than-expected tech earnings reports are heightening concerns that massive investments in AI will not generate the payoff Wall Street expects. Investors are also worried about the debt companies are taking on to finance data center capital expenditures and whether that debt is sustainable.
"Mega-cap stocks have faced increased selling pressure over the past two weeks as elevated AI-related spending and rising financing costs raise concerns over the path to profitability," Adam Turnquist, chief cross-asset strategist for brokerage firm LPL Financial, said in an email. "Recent earnings reports have added to these concerns, revealing slowing growth in select hyperscalers' core businesses."
Another factor weighing on tech stocks is investor expectations that the Federal Reserve will have to keep raising interest rates to curb economic growth and subdue inflation, which remains elevated.
The central bank left its benchmark rate unchanged this week, but many economists think it will hike rates as early as December and into 2027. That would make it more expensive for companies to borrow money to build the data centers required to power AI services, cutting into corporate profits.
Investors have been banking on the explosive growth of AI, which has propelled the stock market to record highs, to continue to dominate. However, that sentiment is now under threat. In a report earlier this week, Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, CIO Americas and global head of equities for UBS' Chief Investment Office, advised clients to "diversify beyond AI."
"While we maintain a constructive outlook on the structural growth of the AI theme, high expectations and potentially wide differences in company outcomes underscore the risks of single-stock concentration," she said. "We think investors should ensure their equity portfolios are broadly diversified."
Still, U.S. stocks remain only 3.4% below their all-time high, boosting the value of workers' 401(k) accounts.
Cryptocurrency prices also slumped after hackers believed to be linked to North Korea stole more than $6 billion from Binance, the world's biggest crypto exchange . The price of bitcoin fell toward $77,000, from more than $86,000 earlier this month.
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

WASHINGTON — President Trump has alleged that elections, public benefit programs and federal grants to nonprofits are rife with fraud. Now, he is increasingly focusing on  fraud in his effort to detain and deport more immigrants.
Recent, high-profile flash points include 28 lawful permanent residents accused this week of illegally voting in California and the federal investigation into Somali-born Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.).
The broader crusade takes many forms, including allegations of fraud in immigration applications , illegal voting by noncitizens and misuse of federal benefits by immigrants who don’t qualify.
“This administration has purposefully mischaracterized immigrants and asylum seekers as fraudsters,” said Royce Murray, a former senior official at the Department of Homeland Security under the Biden administration. That, she said, “serves a narrative that immigrants are not to be trusted and are here to take something rather than contribute, with an end goal of trying to make Americans less welcoming and more comfortable with a mass deportation agenda.”
On Tuesday, Trump and Vice President JD Vance announced a $25-million program under the Justice Department to encourage the public to report suspected fraud in the U.S. government.
This administration has purposefully mischaracterized immigrants and asylum seekers as fraudsters
— Royce Murray, former Department of Homeland Security official
The White House said the first check, for $10,000, will go to right-wing influencer Nick Shirley, who posted a video last year alleging that Somali residents in Minnesota were running fake child-care centers to collect federal subsidies. Dozens of people were convicted in connection with a sprawling, $250-million children’s food assistance scheme that predated this administration, though more charges have been announced in recent months.
Also Tuesday, administration officials launched another nationwide anti-fraud crackdown, this time targeting immigrants who they allege have illegally collected SNAP benefits. Homeland Security highlighted the arrests of five people, calling them “the opening salvo in a sustained, large-scale ICE operation.”
“From day one of my administration, we’ve waged an unprecedented war on corruption and fraud, and will not let our country be looted and plundered by thieves and pirates and foreign fraudsters and basically scum,” Trump said during a news conference announcing the Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program.
Earlier this year, the White House created a task force to eliminate fraud and the Department of Justice created a fraud enforcement division , in part, to target immigration-related offenses. Prosecutors have put aside thousands of other cases to zero in on immigration enforcement.
The focus on fraud has noticeably accelerated in the weeks leading up to the election.
Federal authorities charge 28 people in California with alleged illegal voter registration or voting, escalating the Trump administration’s fight with state election officials.
In California, some of the green card holders arrested this week over voter fraud said they didn’t remember registering to vote. The daughter of one defendant, Omar Muñoz, 72, of Belize, said she wondered whether her father had been confused with his U.S.-born son of the same name, who is a registered voter.
California officials pounced on the small number of people alleged to have cast illegal ballots. Illegal voting by immigrants “is so rare that the Trump admin is parading around town about .0001% of California voters,” Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office wrote on X .
In the last seven weeks alone, the State Department said, 112 noncitizens across 20 states have been charged with illegal voting and registration offenses. Overall, since Trump returned to the White House, 155 people have been charged with voting fraud-related offenses.
Mullin and Atty. Gen. Todd Blanche said earlier this month that Homeland Security agents had secured 10 convictions and detained 100 others for civil immigration violations since August.
During the Biden administration, voter fraud charges were brought in just 13 cases, Blanche added.
Studies and audits of state voter rolls have repeatedly found that voting by noncitizens is rare and hasn’t swayed any elections.
Last week, with mail-in voting already underway, the Justice Department sued California , asking a federal court to bar the state from counting the ballots of 20,000 voters who were flagged by federal officials as “likely noncitizens.” Los Angeles County officials reviewed a sample of 200 of those voter registrations and found that nearly 40% indicated they were born in the U.S.
That number of flagged ballots — 20,000 — is a substantial reduction from the 190,000 noncitizens the administration alleged were on state voter rolls earlier this year, though federal authorities this week said they had found a “separate batch of 17,000 voting records potentially tied to noncitizens.”
California leaders pointed to other states , such as Nevada, where similar accusations have proved meritless.
Murray, the former Homeland Security  official, said she believes the administration is “trying to sow the seeds of doubt that the midterm outcomes will be trustworthy, so that if the Republican Party loses as badly as they’re predicted to, they can characterize it as due to fraud.”
Murray said the Trump administration has largely misconstrued what it means to commit fraud.
“Fraud is a very specific thing — it’s essentially lying,” she said. “Because you don’t get asylum does not mean you committed fraud, it just means you were ineligible.”
In September, a Homeland Security whistleblower told Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) that hundreds of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services employees had been tasked with quickly reviewing the voter information of thousands of people in search of suspected noncitizen voters, and were given a quota of investigating 40 subjects per day.
On Wednesday, a federal judge restricted Homeland Security agents from carrying out sweeping field operations aimed at rooting out voter fraud in nine states, including California.
It is against federal law for immigrants who are not naturalized citizens to vote or register to do so. Penalties can include fines, jail time and even deportation, though authorities rarely pursued that option.
Eric Balliet, a former special agent with Homeland Security Investigations, the criminal investigative arm of ICE, said he takes no issue with investigating fraud, but the timing of this operation and significant resources dedicated show it is “highly politically charged.”
Balliet worked for various administrations, including Trump’s first, before retiring in 2024.  Homeland Security Investigations agents typically focused on transnational criminal investigations such as drug smuggling and human trafficking.
Instead of initiating investigations based on tips or specific information, agents are now taking aggregated data and using algorithms to produce suspect lists, Balliet said. That’s not how law enforcement should operate, he said, calling it a massive privacy overreach against millions of law-abiding citizens.
“It’s the epitome of Big Brother,” he said.
Beyond the allegations of voter fraud, the Trump administration has also increasingly targeted immigrants on suspicion of lying to obtain a visa, green card or citizenship.
Omar’s family fled civil war in Somalia and immigrated to the U.S. in 1995 when she was 12. After agents searched her residence this month looking for evidence that her immigration paperwork contained falsehoods, she called the allegations baseless.

articles.title_orig: G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister
articles.title_zh: G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister
articles.content_orig:
Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov (standing centre) is present at the G20 meeting in Atlanta, US
European diplomats have refused to stand for an official photo with Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in the US, leading to the American hosts cancelling the planned picture.
Two officials confirmed to the BBC the cancellation of the so-called family photo scheduled for Friday morning, which would usually include representatives from all the nations in attendance.
The meeting, which gathers top diplomats from the world's biggest economies, is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Ukraine is not not a G20 member but has been invited to similar meetings in recent years. However, Ukraine was not invited to this meeting.
Relations between Ukraine and the US have been particularly tense this month, with a diplomatic standoff between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and US President Donald Trump over Kyiv's strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is present and a diplomatic source confirmed the UK was among the countries which refused to participate in the picture.
One British official said: "The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine and we are not about to change that".
A US official said the photo was cancelled "after it became clear some of the delegations were unwilling to participate in a joint photo".
"Rather than allow a ceremonial photo opportunity to become a diplomatic distraction, the US decided to forgo the photo and keep the focus on the substantive discussions," the official said.
In contrast to Ukraine, relations between the US and Russia appear to have partially thawed in recent weeks, as Trump waived some sanctions and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the American market.
The move comes as Trump attempts to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of mid-term elections at the start of November, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.
Ukraine and its European allies have heavily criticised Trump's deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Zelensky called it "a gift" to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".
Trump said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table in the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Putin has said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, is willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and currently controls approximately a fifth of Ukrainian territory.
Moscow has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.

articles.title_orig: Italy’s PM deploys troops as nation faces widespread strikes and port blockades
articles.title_zh: Italy’s PM deploys troops as nation faces widespread strikes and port blockades
articles.content_orig:
ROME — Tens of thousands of people were getting ready to take to the streets of Rome, Milan and other Italian cities Friday as part of nationwide demonstrations against the cost of living and high military spending.
After several weeks of violent protests in Italy and throughout Europe , more widespread disruption is expected after the Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) and other trade unions called on workers in both the public and private sectors to strike and protest.
The demonstrations in Italy appear to have been partly inspired by those in France , where some of the worst rioting in decades erupted in cities across the country after student protests about the state of education in the country evolved into wider actions about the cost of living and social security.
Elsewhere in Europe, a huge encampment of tents has occupied a square in Madrid since late last month, and thousands of people in Portugal have taken to the streets in the city of Lisbon. Tear gas and water cannons were also used on black-clad protesters in Brussels.
In Rome, many waved communist and Palestinian flags, as well as signs against the Iran war. Some let off pink smoke bombs. There was a jovial mood among the demonstrators as they lined up before the march, as has often been the case early on at previous protests, only for violence to break out later.
Protesters storm the Colosseum in Rome
Giovanna Di Matteo, a member of the left-wing Potere al Popolo! party, said she was protesting against the government that “did nothing for the people of this country.”
The government had spent money on the military “while they cut on welfare, they cut on services and people cannot reach the end of the month,” she said. “They have no money for their houses, they have no money for gasoline and everything.”
Luca, a 20-year-old medical student said the protesters felt they were “still not being heard, that everything is still the same,” and the government didn’t “care about our voice, about our voices, and about the future of this nation that is our nation.”
“We have been completely screwed by by by the fact that the wages do not keep up on on inflation and the wages in general do not keep up with the corps of living,” added Luca, asked to have his last name withheld out of fear of repercussions from law enforcement.
Major demonstrations also took place in other cities and towns across Italy.
They came after a number of protests in recent weeks have turned violent. Groups of masked protesters looted stores in Milan and elsewhere and threw projectiles at police, who responded with tear gas and water cannons earlier this month.
Italian police were out in force again Friday with riot brigades, drones and helicopters visible in the skies above the Rome protest.
Their presence was heavy after protesters stormed Rome’s historic Colosseum on Saturday, while in the south, farmers and truckers have blockaded highways and ports to protest high fuel prices which have risen since the United States and Israel launched the war against Iran.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni , who has made law and order a key tenet of her administration, said she had “great respect” for peaceful protesters on X earlier this month.
But her right-wing government has since introduced tougher penalties for rioters, including financial liability for parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting.
“There is nothing revolutionary about vandalizing and stealing. Vandalism and theft are not protest, they are criminality,” Meloni said on social media after unveiling the legislation.
The government also said it would deploy 500 army troops alongside the police in Milan until the end of the year.
NBC News Chief Foreign Correspondent
Sara Monetta is a multimedia producer based in London.

articles.content_orig:
Asian trading is mixed as worries about the future of artificial intelligence grow after Alphabet’s stock drop dragged on U.S. markets
TOKYO -- Asian shares were trading mixed Friday, as worries about the future of artificial intelligence grew after Alphabet's stock drop dragged on U.S. markets.
Japan's benchmark Nikkei 225 dropped 2.3% in afternoon trading to 63,155.94. At the end of its two-day monetary policy board meeting, the Bank of Japan decided to keep its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 1.25%. That was widely expected because the central bank raised the rate last month.
The U.S. has been pressuring Japan to raise rates because of concerns about the weakening yen. In currency trading, the U.S. dollar inched up to 157.67 Japanese yen from 157.65 yen. The euro cost $1.1186, up from $1.1181.
Australia's S & P/ASX 200 rose 0.2% to 8,908.10. South Korea's Kospi declined nearly 4% to 5,701.71, as shares in SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics both slipped.
Shares related to the great market interest in AI have tended to be volatile, because some issues, including chip makers, get pushed up because of that interest, but then may decline because of worries about supplies, for instance.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng added 1.7% to 23,359.06, while the Shanghai Composite lost 0.4% to 3,636.60.
On Wall Street, the S & P 500 fell 0.3% for its first loss in four days , even though the wide majority of stocks rose within the index and across Wall Street. The Nasdaq composite tumbled 1.4%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 132 points, or 0.3%.
Alphabet is one of the most influential stocks on Wall Street because it’s one of the largest, and the Class A shares of its stock fell 12.6% for their worst day since they began trading more than 20 years ago.
All told, the S & P 500 fell 23.59 points to 7,720.39 Thursday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 132.54 to 52,342.56, and the Nasdaq composite tumbled 365.13 to 26,184.72.
In the bond market, the yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.94% from 5.05% late Wednesday. It’s been generally pulling back since it topped 5.30% earlier this month and touched its highest level since 2002.
In energy trading, benchmark U.S. crude gained 1.15% to $103.17 a barrel. Brent crude, the international standard, edged up 1.05% to $116.09 a barrel.
AP Business Writer Stan Choe contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia denies report that its CEO was allegedly targeted in Chinese spy plot
articles.title_zh: Nvidia denies report that its CEO was allegedly targeted in Chinese spy plot
articles.content_orig:
The report claimed the CEO was targeted by an executive at Megaspeed.
Nvidia, a top chipmaker, is denying a report that its CEO, Jensen Huang, was allegedly targeted in a Chinese spy plot.
According to a New York Times report published Thursday, U.S. intelligence officials allegedly determined that a top executive at a Singapore-based data center company who developed a "close relationship" with Huang was funneling information to Chinese officials in Beijing.
The executive was identified by the Times as Alice Huang, who was pictured together with the Nvidia CEO in 2024.
Nvidia denied the report in a statement to ABC News, saying Jensen Huang "talks with thousands of customer executives every year."
"Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected," the statement read. "Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job."
A spokesperson for China’s Foreign Ministry also denied the report.
“The reports are baseless and purely slanderous smears against China,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Friday at his daily press briefing.
Neither Alice Huang nor her employer, Megaspeed International, responded to ABC News' request for comment.
According to the Times, President Donald Trump was briefed on U.S. intelligence officials' findings but did not take any action.
The White House has not yet responded to ABC News' request for comment.
Trump is a close ally of Jensen Huang, who has advised the president amid an artificial intelligence race with China. Jensen Huang was a guest at a White House state dinner in September, where Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping.
That same month, the CEO attended a luncheon for AI and tech industry leaders hosted by Trump at the White House.
Earlier this year, in January, Huang convinced the president to clear the way for advance chip sales to China, in a deal that gave the U.S. government 25% of the profits.
Trump also personally owns shares in Nvidia, the world's most publicly traded company.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic may not secure investment-grade rating after IPO, Blackstone tells investors
articles.title_zh: Anthropic may not secure investment-grade rating after IPO, Blackstone tells investors
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic’s S-1 is a new milestone in Big Tech’s sprawling and lofty promises to Wall Street.
Anthropic’s S-1 is a new milestone in Big Tech’s sprawling and lofty promises to Wall Street.
Investing in any stock is kind of like gambling in the sense that you’re betting your money on a company’s future performance. But how do you bet on a technology that could, in the worst-case scenario, “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” or best case, “bring forth an age of miracles”?
To some extent, Anthropic suggests in a letter at the top of its S-1 filing, you have to just believe.
Anthropic’s 335-page S-1 prospectus, filed Monday, is part of a steady hype escalation in Silicon Valley’s interactions with Wall Street. In some ways, it’s not even that bizarre; SpaceX IPO’d in June after filing an S-1 that referenced dinosaurs and “colonizing Mars.” But its sweeping language and sheer volume — including 94 pages of risk factors — is a sometimes overwhelming collision of AI industry rhetoric and a hard financial pitch. Out-of-this-world promises are integral to Anthropic’s survival as a company . That doesn’t make reading the S-1 any less surreal.
In the letter, Anthropic’s founders urge prospective stock owners “not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms. We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater.” The march toward advanced AI “is one of the seminal moments in human history,” the letter says. “Our aim is to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery, and bring forth an age of miracles.” But the S-1 warns that if things go wrong, the consequences could be disastrous — even an “existential” risk to humanity. Many dangers are laid out in exhaustive detail, including risks that models “behave in ways that no user or developer intended,” leading to “catastrophic” incidents that the entire insurance industry couldn’t afford to underwrite.
Tech startups preparing to go public haven’t always used the information overload approach. “In 1980, a highly touted company called Apple Computer went public. Its prospectus, which I have, is 47 pages long with zero risk factors,” said Jay R. Ritter, a professor at the University of Florida’s Warrington College of Business. “If you go back and read it, it’s incredibly simple.”
Ritter pointed to Facebook’s S-1 filing as a turning point. The company now known as Meta filed a 200-page prospectus with 22 pages of risk factors. CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s letter to investors was a manifesto on his move-fast-and-break-things approach to growth, which he dubbed “The Hacker Way.”
While the idea might be to cover all possible bases, “a problem with this bloat is that it’s become more and more difficult to find the nuggets of what’s important,” Ritter said. “You know, I don’t know if you’re like me, but the longer it is, the less inclined I am to read it.”
Anthropic’s founders explain in their investor letter that oversharing is part of their “anti-sell” strategy, designed to attract long-term investors who believe in their vision.
“It is very dangerous when people buy your company’s stock based on expectations you cannot fulfill or on incorrect predictions about how you will behave. This is in fact very similar to one of Anthropic’s guiding principles: underpromise and overdeliver,” the founders’ letter says.
Some of the statements in Anthropic’s S-1 read as surprising admissions. “We may make forward investments that may seem irresponsibly large,” for instance, or “model safety, interpretability, alignment, and welfare may lead us to limit or delay the deprecation of older models.” Maybe none of this should be surprising, considering the founders do warn readers about the company’s policy of practicing “radical honesty.”
Anthropic’s ‘radical honesty’ includes being open about the prospects of human extinction
This policy led to the biggest jumpscare of the whole filing, on page 46:
“Concerns have been raised both within our organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants that, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”
“Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm.”
Anthropic has famously been a proponent of doomsday AI scenarios. CEO Dario Amodei has said there’s an up to 25 percent chance that further AI development could lead to human extinction.
The heart of Anthropic’s pitch — or anti-sell — is that despite the risks, it is absolutely committed to developing safe and secure AI technology. After all, it will go public as a public benefit corporation, a type of business entity that, unlike C-corporations that are required to maximize shareholder value, must prioritize a social mission alongside shareholder interests.
“Powerful AI” — Anthropic’s term for hypothetical future AI that surpasses collective human intelligence — is presented in the company’s S-1 as inevitable. If this technology is coming no matter what, then Anthropic, a public benefit corporation, should lead the charge. But Anthropic will need a lot of money, possibly an unlimited amount, to do this. And more practically, as Liz Lopatto has written , powerful AI (in the form of dramatic recursive self-improvement) might be about the only way Anthropic can stay ahead of the competition and survive.
“All of us have a sincere conviction that the AI exponential will generate so much value, that, in the long run, it will far outweigh any shorter-term economic sacrifices we make as part of our mission,” the letter says.
For all the information the company made available in its S-1, there are some gaps. Crucial information that could be used to assess profitability — third quarter results, for instance — is missing. Anthropic saw explosive revenue growth in the second quarter, but the second quarter was also the height of tokenmaxxing , which could have led to a surge in sales. Some corporate executives have warned that AI costs are surging out of control. While Anthropic’s operating losses narrowed in the second quarter, the S-1 also revealed hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations to secure the computing power it says it needs to keep growing. It also said it will start building its own data center infrastructure, a costly move that would eat into profit.
Ritter thinks Anthropic will likely share its third quarter results the closer it gets to an IPO date. And besides, he added, “nobody knows” what will happen once a company goes public, including the company itself. It’s all a gamble in that sense.
Anthropic isn’t WeWork… although never making money is on its list of risk factors, of course
“For its first 22 years, Apple was largely a failure as far as investors were concerned,” Ritter said. “In its first three years, it greatly underperformed the market. And now it’s worth what, $5 trillion?”
When WeWork filed its S-1 in 2019, it was skewered for using lofty rhetoric. A line about the company’s aim to “elevate the world’s consciousness” was especially roasted.
That was different, Ritter said. WeWork was “a money-losing real estate company pretending to be a tech company at a ridiculously high valuation.”
“There was no chance of ever making huge profits in the future.”
Technically, that’s a risk for Anthropic too. It’s on page 63 of the S-1.
“We have a history of net losses and may not generate sufficient revenue to achieve or sustain profitability in the future.”
Then again, this is the age of miracles.

In contrast to Ukraine, relations between the US and Russia appear to have partially thawed in recent weeks, as Trump waived some sanctions and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the American market.
The move comes as Trump attempts to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of mid-term elections at the start of November, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.
Ukraine and its European allies have heavily criticised Trump's deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Zelensky called it "a gift" to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".
Trump said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table in the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Putin has said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, is willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and currently controls approximately a fifth of Ukrainian territory.
Moscow has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.

articles.title_orig: Tech stocks wipe out more than $1.5 trillion as concerns deepen about the AI boom
articles.title_zh: Tech stocks wipe out more than $1.5 trillion as concerns deepen about the AI boom
articles.content_orig:
Tech stocks plunged Friday, putting the Nasdaq 100 index on course to erase more than $1.5 trillion in value. The index fell 4.2% in afternoon trading, which would represent its worst one-day drop since mid-June.
The broader S&P 500 also dropped sharply, by more than 2.3%. The S&P’s tech sector was by far the worst performing of the day, tumbling by more than 5%.
As trillion-dollar tech companies raise and spend hundreds of billions of dollars to build massive artificial intelligence data centers and develop AI models, investors are on edge as they look for clear signs that all this spending is actually delivering returns.
These questions underpinned one of the day’s worst performing stocks, Intel, which plunged 31%.
Several of Intel’s large peers followed it lower. SanDisk plunged 15%, chipmakers AMD, ARM Holdings, Qualcomm and Marvell all fell 12%, and ASML dropped 7%.
The seeds of Friday’s massive losses were sown Thursday, however, when Amazon and Intel reported quarterly earnings that failed to reassure investors and analysts.
Shares of Amazon declined by as much as 10% in post-market trading Thursday, before recovering throughout the day Friday.
The Philadelphia semiconductor index, of which Intel is a member, sank 9% on Friday. The “DRAM” ETF, which tracks companies linked to computer memory and storage, tumbled 7.2%.
So-called “neocloud” stocks also sold-off. These upstart firms aim to build data centers for software firms to utilize. Nebius and CoreWeave dropped 11%.
The broader Nasdaq Composite, which tracks the more than 3,000 companies that trade on the exchange, fell 3.4%
On Thursday, Amazon reported that its spending to build out AI had continued at a faster clip than expected last quarter, while growth in its core online shopping business had slowed.
The last time Amazon told investors it was upping its AI spending budget, the market rewarded the decision by sending shares up more than 15%.
But a lot has changed in the past three months. Some of the big companies that pay to use AI models have tightened their token budgets. Others have raised questions about exactly how much benefit they’re getting from all the time and resources they’re putting into AI adoption.
In response, some investors are now looking at Big Tech’s massive AI spending through a more skeptical lens .
Nonetheless, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy told shareholders Thursday to brace for even more spending.
“We still expect 2026 cash [capital expenditures] of approximately $220 billion, the majority for AWS, and expect to spend meaningfully more in 2027,” he said on the company’s earnings call. Amazon’s spending had already been set to double from 2025.
Friday’s losses follow significant selling in shares of Alphabet on Thursday .
The Google parent company shed about $500 billion in market value — its worst day ever and the second-worst wipeout of value in market history. On Friday, the stock dropped another 2%.
Intel, meanwhile, told investors that its profits and sales in the fourth quarter would be lower than expected, which sent the stock tanking.
Intel’s stock has surged in recent months as its management implements a sweeping overhaul of the long-ailing chip firm.
In the midst of that turnaround, the U.S. government took a stake in the company , making the federal government the company’s largest shareholder.
Even accounting for Friday’s expected drop, the value of the government’s stake in Intel has grown by 280%.
Analysts at Citigroup described the report as “two steps forward, one step back.”
A major issue highlighted by Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan that contributed to the company’s lackluster performance in the quarter was supply chain issues.
“I’m disappointed that we were not able to meet strong customer demand in this quarter,” Tan told investors on the company’s earnings call. “We face near-term challenges, including manufacturing, supply shortage, the unprecedented memory crunch and the resulting softness in PC demand.”
Meanwhile, the sell-off in tech shares appeared to increase demand for U.S. Treasuries, which briefly sent yields on government bonds lower.
The big AI companies that are borrowing hundreds of billions for data center build-outs have tapped the debt markets for funds, which has in turn created more competition for capital.
As those companies increasingly offer better rates of return for lenders than the U.S. government does on bonds, Treasury yields have risen in recent months — partly to keep up with the private market.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: Traffic Control Errors Caused Spain’s Deadly Train Crash, Official Says
articles.title_zh: Traffic Control Errors Caused Spain’s Deadly Train Crash, Official Says
articles.content_orig:
Oct. 30 (UPI) -- Spain's transportation minister said Friday that he won't resign in the wake of the high-speed train crash that killed at least 69 people Wednesday.
"My duty right now is not to talk about whether I should remain in my position, but to resolve the problem," Óscar Puente said in a press conference in which he said he had "nothing to hide."
Puente has been facing strong criticism and calls to resign after the crash by political rivals.
"The easy thing for me would be to leave, but neither that fits with my character nor is it what the prime minister has asked me to do," he said. "I feel immense pain and immense sadness for the victims and their relatives. ... I cannot let this pain paralyze me though. We have to find solutions to this problem."
The crash happened Wednesday on a rail line between Madrid and Seville, which is popular among tourists. Both trains were shut down due to a computer failure, but the train in the back was told to proceed, while the other train was still stalled, preliminary reports said. The moving train was traveling at between 99 and 124 mph when it crashed into the rear of the stalled train. The conductor of the moving train, in the front car, was killed in the crash.
At least 69 people were killed and dozens more injured. Some residents are still waiting to hear news about their missing relatives.
It's the second train disaster in Spain this year. A train derailment on Jan. 18 killed 46 people.
"It's unacceptable for a country like Spain -- which has such a powerful high-speed rail system -- to experience two accidents of this nature and magnitude within a single year," Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said Friday. "Therefore, our task isn't merely to investigate the causes of what occurred, but also to provide solutions to further strengthen our nation's high-speed rail system. Public trust in the high-speed system has been broken; the government's responsibility goes beyond diagnosing the causes -- it must also offer solutions to ensure that a tragedy of this scale doesn't happen again."
Spain is observing three days of mourning after the accident.

The Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) continues to kill almost half of all those infected in that country, as the official case count now includes 10,141 confirmed cases, including 4,928 related deaths .
World Health Organization (WHO) officials say officials still record 50 to 80 new Ebola cases each day among eight affected DRC provinces, with 80% of cases coming from outside known transmission chains.
Genomic testing released today shows that recent cases in Nigeria and Kenya are from the same genetic group as current cases in DRC, but there is still no understanding of how the patient in Nigeria got infected.
The Nigerian patient visited Uganda from September 15 to October 3. The Kenyan index patient traveled from DRC through Uganda from October 1 to October 3. Both patients were at the Entebbe airport in Uganda on October 3. Both samples collected from the index patients do not carry any markers of the Ugandan Ebola cases reported in May and June of this year, eliminating the suggesting of underreported spread in that country. Instead, both carry the same genetic lineage as cases in the DRC.
Kenya has confirmed nine cases and two deaths, while no additional Ebola patients have been identified in Nigeria.
Although the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says Americans are at a low risk in the outbreak, the agency announced a new rule today stating all passengers boarding an international flight to the United States must attest via a signed statement that they have not been in the DRC during the previous 21 days.
The required attestation will begin on November 3 and last through December 18.
Travelers, including U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals, who have been in DRC within 21 days before their flight will not be allowed to board flights with U.S. destinations.
“Travelers, including U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals, who have been in DRC within 21 days before their flight will not be allowed to board flights with U.S. destinations and should plan to remain outside the United States for at least 21 days after they leave DRC,” the CDC said. “This includes all passengers transiting through DRC on a connecting flight regardless of whether they disembark or stay on the airplane.”
The CDC said about 500 people at the agency are involved in responding to the outbreak, including more than 120 people deployed to the affected countries.
Today Director-General Jean Kaseya, MD, MPH, of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, warned that the Ebola outbreak could spread to the United Kingdom and other European countries.
“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented,” he said . “Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.”
The CDC says drug-resistant bacteria and fungi cause 9.7 million infections and 50,800 US deaths a year.
High levels of intestinal inflammation are linked to post-vaccination fever.
The state had not seen the disease in decades.
The gap between the diseases we fear and the actual dangers we face is significant. This Halloween, CIDRAP Director Michael Osterholm outlines the public health threats that worry him most.

The second patient to die in Kenya was a close relative of the index patient.
But the University of Minnesota epidemiologist says the recognition belongs to a much larger group.
At the same time, confidence in the safety of longstanding vaccines, including MMR and polio, remains high.
The province has the world’s highest rates of the fatal neurodegenerative disease in animals such as deer, elk, and moose.

ExxonMobil Profits Double to $15.4 Billion

Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her…
ExxonMobil reported $15.4 billion in third-quarter profit Friday, more than double its earnings a year earlier, with its Gulf Coast refineries running at full capacity and diesel prices doing the rest.
The company earned $3.72 per share, or $4.23 on an adjusted basis, beating Wall Street's $4.08 estimate. Adjusted net income reached $17.5 billion, making it one of Exxon's most profitable quarters ever.
Exxon's energy products business earned $9.05 billion in adjusted profit, up from $4.1 billion in the second quarter. Its U.S. Gulf Coast refinery units operated at 100% utilization, producing their second-highest diesel volumes on record.
The Iran war and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have sidelined roughly 10% of global refining capacity, leaving the remaining plants to supply a market desperately short of diesel and other fuels. Refining margins have soared, and Exxon is certainly making the most of them.
The company has also increased the amount of fuel it can produce. Its Gulf Coast distillate output is up approximately 40% since 2019, helped by the $2 billion Beaumont refinery expansion completed in 2023. That project added 250,000 barrels per day of processing capacity, an investment approved years before today's fuel shortage.
Exxon's upstream business had a less impressive quarter. Adjusted earnings fell to $7.3 billion from $9.2 billion in the second quarter as crude prices eased. Production held near 4.5 million barrels of oil equivalent per day.
Exxon generated $25.7 billion in operating cash flow and returned $9.4 billion to shareholders through dividends and stock repurchases, including $5.1 billion in buybacks. It also increased its dividend for the 44th consecutive year and announced plans for another $20 billion in share repurchases in 2027.
With Exxon's Gulf Coast refineries already operating at full capacity, further production increases will be difficult without additional investment. Global diesel supplies remain constrained by refinery damage in the Middle East and Russia, even as crude shipments from the Persian Gulf recover.
By Julianne Geiger for Oilprice.com

articles.title_orig: China expels record number of officials from CCP
articles.title_zh: China expels record number of officials from CCP
articles.content_orig:
The unprecedented number of empty seats at the fifth plenum – a symbol of expulsions – serve as a symbol for the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping
China expelled a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP) as it concluded a major political gathering , which saw an unprecedented number of empty seats indicating the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping.
A record 33 members were expelled at this week’s fifth plenum, a gathering of top officials that takes place roughly once a year.
Just 279 of the full and alternate members of the CCP’s Central Committee attended this week’s gathering, compared with the 376 originally named as members in 2022. That means that more than 25% of the original cohort were absent, many due to purges. It is the highest number of “empty chairs” at the plenum in modern Chinese history.
The confirmed expulsions included Zhang Youxia, the former second-in-command to China’s leader in the military hierarchy, and Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang. Other absences were unexplained.
“More empty seats underscores the plenum’s focus on Xi’s vision of strict internal discipline,” said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, in a post on X.
The theme for this week’s plenum was party governance. Since coming to power in 2012 Xi has focused on stamping out corruption in the party. But in recent years the campaign has intensified , taking out officials in the highest ranks of the party and the military, raising questions about if the campaign is also a tool to remove political rivals or punish disloyalty.
Xi appears to have grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a lack of discipline in the ranks of the party that wields absolute authority over the state and society in China. Earlier this year he said that the party must uproot “sick trees” and that the fight against corruption was a “never-ending journey”.
A series of purges has gutted the seven-man Central Military Commission, the ruling body of China’s People’s Liberation Army. There are now just two members left: Xi himself, and the military’s anti-graft tsar, Zhang Shengmin.
Zhang was promoted to the politburo of the CCP this week, the highest ruling body in the party. Zhang is now the only military member of the senior leadership body.
The plenum also laid the groundwork for the 21st Party congress, an event which happens every five years and is expected to next be held in the second half of 2027. Xi, who is already the longest ruler of Communist China since Mao Zedong, is expected to secure a fourth term as party leader.
The ranks of the Central Committee and the politburo will be refreshed at next year’s congress, but many analysts believe that recent purges have been so wide-ranging that there are few suitable candidates to be promoted.

articles.title_orig: The Scrapyard Search for Rare Earths
articles.title_zh: The Scrapyard Search for Rare Earths
articles.content_orig:
The technology recovers valuable rare-earth materials and converts them into reusable compounds that can be used in the production of new magnets, supporting a more circular and resilient European supply chain.
For these reasons, the International Sustainable Chemistry Collaborative Centre (ISC3) has chosen TSR Innovations as one of the finalists of the ISC3 Innovation Challenge 2026 and the start-up is featured as the ISC3 Start-up of the Month for October 2026.
A key aspect of the innovation is its use of mechanochemistry, which uses mechanical forces to drive chemical transformations. Unlike many conventional recycling routes, the process operates with low energy and chemical requirements and is designed to process complex waste streams that are often difficult to recycle using existing methods. By recovering valuable rare-earth materials that might otherwise be lost, TSR Innovations helps reduce resource waste and creates a secondary source of critical raw materials for future production.
From a sustainability perspective, the technology offers several advantages. According to the company, it can operate at room temperature and normal pressure. In addition, its modular design could enable deployment closer to collection points or manufacturing sites, reducing transportation needs and strengthening regional circular-economy ecosystems.
The whole success story of the ISC3 Start-up of the Month in October 2026 is currently told by the ISC3 on its website at TSR Innovations (isc3.org) .
Three questions for Tomislav Stolar (Founder and CEO of TSR Innovations)
What led you to found TSR Innovations and develop a solution in Sustainable Chemistry?
Tomislav Stolar: Mechanochemistry is a branch of chemistry that uses mechanical forces, such as those in ball milling, to drive chemical transformations. Most mechanochemical processes give high yields and run at room temperature and pressure without the need for heating or pressurization. Hence, mechanochemistry is time-, energy-, and reagent-efficient and is highly disruptive to traditional chemical manufacturing and recycling. After decades of extensive community research on mechanochemistry, I believed there was little industry application to show for it. Consequently, I took the initiative to start TSR Innovations and commercialize a mechanochemical recycling process for rare-earth magnets.
What does being chosen as ISC3 Start-up of the Month mean to you?
T. Stolar: Honestly, it means a ton. So far, we have been working in stealth on purpose, but we're now ready to move fast. ISC3 is helping us with that. We are excited about the journey ahead.
What's next up at TSR Innovations?
T. Stolar: We are ready to move from the lab to pilot scale and to significantly expand the core team. In the long term, we want to realize the first European small and modular mechanochemical long-loop recycling plant and help Europe achieve rare earth supply chain independence.

articles.title_orig: Police Scotland carrying out 'active inquiries' into Andrew and Epstein Balmoral visits
articles.title_zh: Police Scotland carrying out 'active inquiries' into Andrew and Epstein Balmoral visits
articles.content_orig:
Police Scotland is making inquiries into the activities of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislane Maxwell during their time at Balmoral Castle.
The Daily Express reported that the inquiry relates to allegations that women were trafficked to the royal residence in Aberdeenshire.
Sex offender Epstein - who died in 2019 - and Maxwell, who was jailed in 2022 for sex trafficking , are understood to have visited the castle with Mountbatten-Windsor, who has previously denied any wrongdoing.
Police Scotland said inquiries were at "a very early stage" and that it would be inappropriate to comment further.
Representatives of Mountbatten-Windsor have been contacted for comment.
The Royal family traditionally spend summer at Balmoral, where Queen Elizabeth II died in 2022.
Asked about the Express report, a Police Scotland spokesperson said: "We have received information and active inquiries are ongoing but these are at a very early stage.
"All inquiries are evidence led, with the needs of victim survivors at the heart of those inquiries.
"We would never confirm details of ongoing inquiries and it would be inappropriate to comment further."
In February, the force said it wanted to "speak to anyone with information" about Epstein's private jet using Edinburgh Airport.
At the time officers said they had not received any reports or complaints in relating to the trip.
Flight logs show Mountbatten-Windsor and Maxwell flew from Luton to Edinburgh on Epstein's private jet with two other passengers on 1 September 2006.
An image believed to show disgraced financier Epstein and former socialite Maxwell at Balmoral was also released by US prosecutors during her sex trafficking trial.
It is thought to have been taken in 1999, when Mountbatten-Windsor reportedly invited the couple to stay at the castle.
Epstein and Maxwell were reportedly regular guests at royal residences in the late 1990s and early 2000s.
Last year, the so-called Epstein Files were released by the US Department of Justice.
Among them was an email from someone named 'A' to Maxwell which said they were at Balmoral and asked for "new inappropriate friends".
The message, sent to Maxwell on 16 August 2001, begins: "I am up here at Balmoral Summer Camp for the Royal Family."
Later in the email, the sender asks: "How's LA? Have you found me some new inappropriate friends?" before signing off "see ya A xxx".
Jeffrey Epstein was 66 when he died by suicide in 2019 in a US prison while awaiting trial for sex trafficking charges.
Maxwell, 60, was jailed for 20 years in 2022 for her role in procuring girls for Epstein.
Last October it was confirmed Andrew had been stripped of his "prince" title and would be leaving his Windsor mansion, Royal Lodge.
In February he was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office , in the wake of information that emerged from the Epstein files in the US, and later released.
Earlier this month it emerged he was taking legal action against Thames Valley Police over search warrants issued before his arrest.
Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied any wrongdoing linked to his association with Epstein.
Asked about the latest reports, Scottish First Minister John Swinney said: "I understand the seriousness of the points that have been made and the concern that has been expressed.
"This is an operational matter for Police Scotland to fully and comprehensively investigate and I'm very confident that's exactly what Police Scotland will do."
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he did not want to comment on the police inquiries, which "should properly be independent".
